1) Blocking I/O:
For example, read() waits until a message arrives.
Why not create a thread and leave it waiting? That seems reasonable from a client perspective.
But if a server does the same, every socket connection needs its own blocking-I/O thread.
2) Nonblocking I/O:
read() returns immediately. Often no message is available, so it returns -1 and sets errno to EWOULDBLOCK, indicating that no data is ready.
We need a mechanism to know when data arrives before calling read(). One crude approach continually polls the function, reading as soon as data appears.
3) I/O multiplexing:
This improves on blocking I/O. Before read(), select examines all sockets for messages, blocking until one becomes ready. Then a blocking read copies the message from the kernel into the process.
4) Signal-driven I/O:
This partly asynchronous model first calls a signal-related system function to associate a socket with a signal, then returns without waiting. The kernel checks for data and signals the process when it is available. The process then calls blocking read() to copy data from the kernel. Registration is nonblocking; the read blocks.
5) Asynchronous I/O:
You may already see an improvement. Like the preceding model, associate the socket with a signal, also providing a data buffer, then return immediately. The kernel checks for data, fills the supplied buffer and triggers the signal. The process responds and reads directly from the buffer, with no blocking throughout.
Our CocoaAsyncSocket framework clearly uses this fifth model.
